title: How to Reset an HVAC System Safely
h1: How Do I Reset My HVAC System?
description: Learn how to safely reset your HVAC system at the thermostat, breaker and furnace switch, how long to wait before restarting, and when a reset is not enough.
quick_answer: Turn the system off at the thermostat, switch off the breaker for the outdoor unit and the furnace or air handler switch, and wait about 5 minutes. Turn power back on, then set the thermostat to call for heat or cooling. If it shuts down again or trips the breaker, stop resetting it and have it checked.
body:
When does resetting an HVAC system help?

A reset clears the electronics and gives the system a fresh start. It can fix problems caused by a power outage, a brief voltage dip, a thermostat that's lost its connection, or a furnace control board that locked out after a few failed starts.

A reset won't fix a broken part. If the system keeps shutting off, the reset is just covering up the real problem, and repeated restarts can make some failures worse.

What should I check before resetting?

Many "my AC won't turn on" calls end up being one of these, so check them first:

  • Thermostat settings. Make sure it's set to Heat or Cool, not Off or Fan, and that the setpoint is above or below room temperature.
  • Thermostat batteries. A blank or dim screen often just means new batteries.
  • The air filter. A badly clogged filter can cause the system to overheat or freeze up and shut down.
  • The furnace door. Most furnaces have a safety switch that cuts power if the front panel isn't seated properly.
  • The condensate drain. Many systems have a float switch that shuts things down when the drain pan fills up.

How do I reset my HVAC system step by step?

  1. Turn the thermostat to Off.
  2. Turn off power to the indoor unit. Look for a light-switch-style service switch on or near the furnace or air handler. In San Diego and Orange County homes, that's usually in the garage, attic or a hall closet.
  3. Turn off the breaker for the outdoor AC or heat pump at the main electrical panel. There may also be a disconnect box on the wall next to the outdoor unit.
  4. Wait about 5 minutes. This lets the compressor pressures settle and gives the control boards time to fully reset.
  5. Turn the breaker and service switch back on.
  6. Set the thermostat to Heat or Cool with a setpoint a few degrees past room temperature.
  7. Give it several minutes. Many systems have a built-in delay before the compressor or burner starts.

Some outdoor units and furnaces have a reset button, but don't press it over and over. A tripped safety is telling you something.

How do I reset a smart or programmable thermostat?

Sometimes the thermostat is the part that needs a reset, not the equipment. Smart thermostats can lose Wi-Fi, get stuck in an eco or away mode, or run an old schedule after an update. Try restarting it from the settings menu, or pull it gently off the wall plate for 30 seconds and snap it back on.

A full factory reset erases your schedule and wiring setup, so save it for last. Take a photo of the wiring before you remove a thermostat from its base, and if the screen still stays blank with good batteries, the problem may be a blown low-voltage fuse at the furnace, which is a job for a technician.

What if the breaker keeps tripping?

A breaker that trips once after an outage may be a fluke. A breaker that trips again right after you reset it points to an electrical problem, such as a failing compressor, a bad capacitor, a shorted fan motor or loose wiring. Leave it off and call for service. Resetting a breaker repeatedly can damage the equipment and is a fire risk.

The same goes for a furnace that keeps locking out. Many furnaces flash an error code on the control board, visible through a small window in the panel. Write it down before you call, because it helps the technician narrow down the problem.

When should I call a technician instead?

Stop and call for help if you notice any of the following:

  • The system shuts down again within minutes or hours of a reset
  • You hear buzzing, grinding or clicking from the outdoor unit but the fan doesn't spin
  • The indoor coil or refrigerant lines are covered in ice
  • You see water around the furnace or air handler
  • You smell burning or electrical odors

If you ever smell gas, don't touch any switches. Leave the house and call the gas utility from outside. If a carbon monoxide alarm goes off, get everyone out and call 911.

For anything beyond a simple reset, our HVAC repair technicians can track down the cause. During the first hot inland stretch of the year or the first cold nights in late fall, it's also a good idea to have a tune-up so small issues don't become shutdowns.
faqs: How long should I wait to reset my HVAC system?
About 5 minutes with the power off is enough for most systems. That gives the compressor pressures time to equalize and lets the control boards fully reset before you restart.
Where is the reset button on my AC?

Most central AC systems don't have a single reset button. The reset is done by cycling power at the breaker and the indoor service switch. Some furnaces and heat pumps have a reset on the control board, but repeated use isn't a fix.
Why did my AC stop working after a power outage?

Outages and the surge when power returns can trip a breaker, scramble the thermostat or put the control board into a lockout. A full power reset often fixes it. If not, a component may have been damaged and should be checked.
Is it safe to reset my HVAC system myself?

Yes, turning off the thermostat, service switch and breaker is safe for homeowners. Don't open electrical panels on the units, bypass safety switches or keep resetting a breaker that trips. Those are signs of a problem a technician should handle.
